name: Grape wine making, Kvemo Kartli, Georgia
summary: Grape wine made in early Neolithic villages in Georgia about 6000–5800 BC, the earliest chemically confirmed grape wine from the Near East.
description: Sherds of large Neolithic jars from two villages of the Shulaveri-Shomutepe culture, Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora in Kvemo Kartli, Georgia, tested positive for tartaric acid, the marker of grape and wine, together with malic, succinic and citric acids. The authors date this evidence to about 6000 to 5800 BC and take the jars to have served for fermenting, ageing and serving wine.

impact.note: Reach 1 because the paper says priority among Near Eastern regions cannot be assigned, so the descent of later wine cultures from these villages is unproven and only the South Caucasus is counted; wine was a new storable drink and substance of ritual and exchange (depth 2); a few direct successors in regional viniculture (generativity 1).

date.label: ca. 6000–5800 BC
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Chemical analysis of pottery from early Neolithic sites in Georgia (Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora) gives evidence of grape wine and viniculture at about 6000 to 5800 BC.

evidence.supports: provide the earliest biomolecular archaeological evidence for grape wine and viniculture from the Near East, at ca. 6,000–5,800 BC

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Hajji Firuz Tepe in Iran, whose wine jars the paper places half a millennium later, and the Areni-1 winery in Armenia were not researched and may deserve their own records.
Whether the grapes were cultivated or wild: the sites lie within the range of the wild Eurasian grape, and the paper calls for more excavation and DNA analysis of wild vines.
The place is the province; the two villages lie within 2 km of each other about 50 km south of Tbilisi, and their exact coordinates were not taken from a gazetteer.

research.note: Asked which region has priority in the discovery and spread of the wine culture and the domesticated grape, the authors answer that 'It is impossible to assign priority to any of these regions at this stage in the investigation', so neither independence nor derivation is established.
